name: Great Plains
label: Homestead
lede: A Columbus band that wrote about Rutherford B. Hayes, Lincoln Logs and record-store clerks, on a label that mostly forgot to pay them.

eras.title: Columbus, before the records
eras.text: Ron House had already fronted Moses Carryout, Twisted Shouts and Ron & the True Believers. In 1981 he started a band with two brothers and a drummer, and spent two years becoming Great Plains.

years.src: Wikipedia: Ron House · Grokipedia: Great Plains
years.h: [[Ron House|f6375d7a-1ad5-4ae6-a86b-6fcfcd9763c0]] starts Great Plains in Columbus with the Wyatt brothers
years.p: Matt Wyatt plays guitar, Mark Wyatt plays organ, Dave Green drums, and Don Howland (Hank O'Hare) holds down bass.
years.xp:
House came to Columbus from Wooster to attend Ohio State and had already cycled through Moses Carryout, Twisted Shouts and Ron & the True Believers. Great Plains was the first of his bands to stick.

Grokipedia credits Howland on bass from 1981 to 1983 and lists Mike Hummel, Paul Nini and Jim Castoe as the bassists who followed. It says Green went by "Manic."

years.src: Wikipedia: Great Plains (Ohio band) · Trouser Press: Great Plains · The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio
years.h: The Mark, Don & Mel EP: eight songs on New Age
years.p: Great Plains' first record came out on the small New Age label, before Homestead entered the picture.
years.xp:
Wikipedia lists it as an eight-track EP. Trouser Press titles it The Mark, Don & Me!. The band's own Bandcamp reissue calls it "Mark, Don & Mel."

The American Prospect names "Pretty Dictionary" among its songs. Matt Wyatt later told the magazine the early sessions happened in a studio built for commercial jingles, where the band was "shuttled off into our little booths."

eras.title: Homestead takes them in
eras.text: Homestead Records, a Long Island sublabel run by Gerard Cosloy, puts out the first two Great Plains LPs. The history-nerd songwriting arrives.

years.src: Robert Christgau: Great Plains · Wikipedia: Homestead Records · Bandcamp Daily: How Homestead Records
years.h: Born in a Barn: the first Great Plains LP, on Homestead
years.p: Robert Christgau gave it a B+ and noted that each folk-punk arrangement stands apart.
years.xp:
Homestead began in 1983 as a sublabel of the Long Island distributor Dutch East India Trading. Founder Sam Berger left in 1984 and Gerard Cosloy, who had made the fanzine Conflict, became its sole employee.

Bandcamp Daily counts Great Plains among Homestead's initial roster. Wikipedia adds that the label was known for poor communication with artists and for unpaid royalties.

years.src: Vice: Straight to Vinyl, Finally · Bandcamp Daily: How Homestead Records · Robert Christgau: Great Plains · Trouser Press: Great Plains
years.h: Naked at the Buy, Sell and Trade and the record-store clerk song
years.p: "Letter to a Fanzine" needles indie-shop clerks and the labels they pledge loyalty to; Bandcamp Daily and Vice both single it out.
years.xp:
Vice calls "Letter to a Fanzine" one of the best meta-commentaries on the underground. Bandcamp Daily describes a needling guitar hook over washes of organ. Christgau gave the album a B+ and called its organ-driven songs "objectively boring" and hummable anyway.

Dates disagree. Wikipedia and Trouser Press say 1985; Christgau, the American Prospect and the band's own Bandcamp say 1986.
play: Naked at the Buy, Sell and Trade

years.src: The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio
years.h: Live at the Electric Banana, Pittsburgh, 5.22.85
years.p: A recording of this Pittsburgh show survives, and the American Prospect says it beats the studio versions of several songs.
years.xp:
Mark Wyatt told the Prospect that how a show went "depended on Ron's blood-alcohol level," and that set lists were hastily written down and then often discarded.

House himself called Great Plains live a high-wire act.

years.src: Furious: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments interview
years.h: Opening for the Replacements, more than once
years.p: House says Great Plains played support slots for [[The Replacements|dc0d05ce-2f47-4962-b4fa-8631a0a51987]] during these years.
years.xp: In a Furious interview, House places the band's start in a moment around 1982 when things were turning toward American roots music, and names the [[The Embarrassment|487904ff-d3ef-477e-813a-c27548bc0570]] and the Gun Club as reference points.

eras.title: American history, plugged in
eras.text: House reads Edmund Wilson's Civil War book and starts writing about presidents, ballplayers and Serpent Mound. The band gets louder, and critics split on whether that helped.

years.src: The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio · Erasing Clouds: Great Plains
years.h: Rutherford B. Hayes, Lincoln Logs and the Black Sox
years.p: House's songs pull from Edmund Wilson's Patriotic Gore and 19th-century Ohio politics: "Rutherford B. Hayes," "Lincoln Logs," "Black Sox Scandal."
years.xp:
The American Prospect lists "Dick Clark," "Black Like Me," "Origin of My Silly Grin" and "Serpent Mound" alongside them. It credits House's reading in Wilson's Patriotic Gore, post-structuralism and Ohio political history.

Reviewer Dave Heaton later heard dirty punk rock "in the Ohio sense," with new wave melody.

years.src: Robert Christgau: Great Plains · Trouser Press: Great Plains · Wikipedia: Great Plains (Ohio band)
years.p: His best grade for the band, with a comparison to Tom Waits and advice to catch them live.
years.xp:
Trouser Press reviewer Ira Robbins thought the later records suffered from overproduction and louder arrangements. Christgau disagreed and praised House's literary ambitions.

Wikipedia and Trouser Press date the LP 1987; the band's Bandcamp says 1988. A Before We Stop to Think EP is also dated 1987.

eras.title: Momentum gone
eras.text: By the end of the decade, House says the shows weren't fun and Homestead had lost interest. The band ends in 1989.

q: I noticed that the momentum had gone.
years.src: Furious: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments interview · Bandcamp Daily: How Homestead Records
years.h: Great Plains ends after eight years
years.p: Ron House told Furious he was ready to give up music, and that Homestead cared less than in '85.
years.xp: House also said, "We never really got to be that famous." Cosloy, who signed the band, resigned from Homestead in 1990 and went on to co-found Matador.

years.p: A 1989 collection on Diabolo Records, listed by Wikipedia among the band's last releases.

eras.title: Uncaring on purpose
eras.text: House starts a new band and swears off worrying what anyone thinks, then lands on a major label anyway.

years.cap: Ron House with Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments
years.src: Furious: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments interview · Wikipedia: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments
years.h: [[Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments|e20ec776-cbfb-43f9-8659-d1c4f373bec5]] start with Ron House
years.p: House says he wanted to make music without caring what everybody thought about it.
years.xp: Wikipedia dates the band to 1989, with guitarist Bob Petric among the core members. The name refers to Thomas Jefferson's slave quarters at Monticello.

years.h: House lands on American Recordings with an $800 record
years.p: Bait and Switch by Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments comes out via Onion Records and American Recordings.
years.xp: Wikipedia says it was recorded for $800. Christgau gave it an A− and said the opening songs rush by in a perfect furious tunefest.

eras.title: The catalog comes back
eras.text: Old 3C Records reissues the Homestead-era work, and the songs go online in full.

years.src: Robert Christgau: Length of Growth · Erasing Clouds: Great Plains · The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio
years.h: Length of Growth 1981-89: 50 songs on two discs
years.p: Christgau's B+ came with a candid note that not all of it is great and some is barely good.
years.xp:
Old 3C Records issued it. The American Prospect dates it 2000; Wikipedia and Christgau say 2001. The Prospect follows it with Cornflakes (2003), an odds and ends collection, and says Old 3C was run by a former Great Plains bassist.

Wikipedia names that bassist Paul Nini; the Prospect calls him Paul Wyatt.

years.h: Ron House releases his first solo album, Obsessed
years.p: It comes out on his own Moses Carryout Records; during the 1990s he also became part owner of Columbus's Used Kids record store.

years.h: Great Plains play live on WFMU
years.p: A Free Music Archive listing shows a live set including "Letter to a Fanzine" on WFMU's Cherry Blossom Clinic, 8/22/2008.

years.h: Counter Intuits: House with Jared Phillips of Times New Viking
years.p: Sheets of Hits (2013) and Monosyllabilly (2016) come out on House's Pyramid Scheme imprint.

years.src: Great Plains Bandcamp: Length of Growth 1981-89 (vol. 1) · Great Plains Bandcamp: Length of Growth 1981-89 (vol. 2)
years.h: Great Plains put their catalog on Bandcamp
years.p: Both volumes of Length of Growth 1981-89 are released August 5, 2020: 24 tracks on vol. 1, 27 on vol. 2.
